clinicalVerdict: Correct on both blanks. The triad of new anisocoria, vomiting and a fall in level of orientation after an unwitnessed fall in an anticoagulated older adult is the classic presentation demanding urgent evaluation for intracranial haemorrhage, and the case supplies each element rather than implying it. A shortened, externally rotated limb is the textbook sign of a displaced proximal femoral fracture, so the conjunction keyed in dropdown 1 is right. Keyed dropdown 2 is right and is the safe nursing action: with a suspected fracture and a possible head injury the resident is kept still under spinal and limb precautions pending imaging. All four distractors are genuinely and specifically wrong rather than filler, and each is defeated by a fact the chart establishes - the chronic-dementia option by the documented baseline orientation, the low-risk-bruising option by the unwitnessed fall and the neurologic findings, and both action distractors by the fracture signs. I found no invented fact, no stranded value, no key ambiguity and no all-correct degeneracy.
